startup.name: OpenRelay
startup.description: No description was given beyond the one liner. A two person team building a way to run AI inference across distributed and mixed hardware. Buyers would be teams that want cheaper or more available inference.

yc_acceptance.basis: Note only because the company is already accepted. A random applicant starts near 1 percent. A two person team in AI infrastructure with no stated traction would be near the base, lifted by the strong market pull for inference and any technical founder pedigree.
yc_acceptance.why_it_fails: YC would most plausibly say no because the pitch is one line in a space crowded with funded inference clouds, and distributed inference has a long record of latency, trust and reliability problems. Without a named customer or a demo of mixed hardware beating a single cloud on cost, reviewers would see a clever architecture with no buyer.

ladder.why_it_fails: The seed stalls if the team cannot show that distributed inference on mixed hardware beats a plain managed provider on cost and reliability. Investors have seen decentralized compute pitches fail on latency and trust, and a two person team has little time to prove it. Analogs such as Mystic and Pipeshift raised only small seeds after similar low latency inference pitches.

ladder.why_it_fails: A Series B needs scale in production traffic and gross margins that hold against price cuts by the big inference clouds. If the network depends on third party hardware with variable quality, margins and uptime suffer. Few analogs reached B, and those that did had a differentiated moat such as kernel optimization.

ladder.why_it_fails: The company stops before C if the largest inference providers keep lowering prices and absorb most demand. A hardware agnostic layer can be commoditized by cloud and chip vendors who offer the same portability, leaving only a niche of cost sensitive workloads. Investors would also compare the company with the closest analogs in the data, most of which stalled at this step without clear revenue or a durable advantage over better funded rivals.

outcomes.why_it_fails: Most paths fail because inference is a price war led by well funded providers, and a distributed network adds latency and trust problems. If no customer needs hardware agnosticism enough to pay, the team stalls after the seed and ends as an acquihire by a compute company. Investors would also compare the company with the closest analogs in the data, most of which stalled at this step without clear revenue or a durable advantage over better funded rivals.

killers.risk: Inference prices fall faster than a distributed network can match
killers.evidence: Large providers raised billions in 2026 and compete on price and speed, which pushes margins toward zero for undifferentiated capacity.
killers.mitigation: Compete on a measurable niche such as sovereign or privacy sensitive workloads, not on raw price.

killers.risk: Latency, reliability and trust issues on distributed hardware
killers.evidence: Enterprise buyers need guarantees that mixed and remote nodes struggle to give, and similar decentralized pitches stayed small.
killers.mitigation: Offer only workloads tolerant of delay, such as batch jobs, and publish uptime numbers.

killers.risk: Two person team and a one line pitch with no customer
killers.evidence: Seed investors need a demo or design partner and the listing has no description.
killers.mitigation: Ship an open source runtime and sign two design partners in the first 90 days.

killers.risk: Chip and cloud vendors add hardware portability
killers.evidence: Gimlet Labs and General Compute already build multi chip inference layers with large funding.
killers.mitigation: Build a data or integration moat with early customers.

technical_complexity.rationale: Scheduling inference across mixed hardware, keeping latency predictable and verifying results from untrusted nodes are hard distributed systems problems. A two person team can build a prototype but not an enterprise grade network in three months, so the hard parts are a risk before they are a moat.

takeover_risk.rationale: Funded inference platforms can add hardware portability quickly and already have customers and capital. A distributed variant is harder to copy, but the buyer is likely to be satisfied by a managed provider.

evidence.claim: Inference demand is surging and investors funded Baseten at $13B in June 2026.
DeepInfra raised $107M in May 2026 to expand a dedicated inference cloud.

brand.rationale: A descriptive compound that fits a network of nodes. Compound names show no survival difference in the cohort data and developer infrastructure rarely depends on the name, though a generic one makes search and trademark harder.

narrative.headline: A thin one line pitch in the hottest and most crowded part of AI infrastructure, with a coin flip on seed and low odds beyond.
narrative.general_summary: OpenRelay promises distributed, hardware agnostic inference. Demand for inference is large in mid 2026 and billion dollar companies prove it, but those companies already serve the buyers with managed clouds. A seed above the YC check is about as likely as the cohort base rate because AI infrastructure is funded and the team is early. The team must show a cost or sovereignty advantage that managed providers do not offer. Reaching Series A needs production revenue, and the price war makes that hard. About 55 percent of forecast paths end in a stall or shutdown.
